# Testing Differences

We previously found that more deprived LSOAs tend to have somewhat higher levels of NO~2~. Last week, we saw that a sample never matches the population exactly. This week, we bring the two together. When we see a difference between two groups in a sample, how do we know whether it reflects a real difference in the population, or whether it could simply be the result of which LSOAs happened to end up in our sample? This is the question a **hypothesis test** tries to answer.

You already ran a t-test in Term 1. This week, we will look at what such a test actually does, what its result does and does not tell us, and how to report it. This session links to the second statistics worksheet, so you can use the time in class to make a start on your own analysis.

::: {.callout-important}
## Before the session
Open your `GEOG0187-stats` project. Create a new script, `w07-testing.R`. Have a look back at [Confidence intervals]({{< var urls.w06 >}}#confidence-intervals) from last week.
:::

## Pollution and deprivation in Outer London
We also found that the link between income deprivation and NO~2~ looked different in Inner and Outer London. In this session, we will focus on Outer London and look at whether LSOAs in the most income-deprived fifth of London are exposed to higher levels of NO~2~ than LSOAs in the least deprived fifth.

Just like last week, we will pretend that we cannot measure every LSOA and instead only have data for a random sample: in this case, 30 LSOAs from each group. Because we do in fact have data for all LSOAs, we can check at the end how close our sample got to the true answer.

Let us start by loading the data, adding the income deprivation quintiles we created before, and selecting the two groups we want to compare:

```{r}
#| label: 07-load
#| filename: 'R code'
#| message: false
# load the tidyverse and the data
library(tidyverse)
lsoa <- read_csv('data/london-lsoa-air-quality.csv')

# income deprivation quintiles across London, as before
lsoa <- lsoa |>
  mutate(income_quintile = ntile(income_score, 5))

# Outer London, least (1) and most (5) deprived fifths only
outer <- lsoa |>
  filter(inner_outer == 'Outer', income_quintile %in% c(1, 5)) |>
  mutate(group = if_else(income_quintile == 5, 'Most deprived', 'Least deprived'),
         group = factor(group, levels = c('Most deprived', 'Least deprived')))

# a random sample of 30 LSOAs from each group
set.seed(48)
my_sample <- outer |>
  group_by(group) |>
  slice_sample(n = 30) |>
  ungroup()
```

::: {.callout-note}
The `factor()` function with `levels` fixes the order of the two groups. This means R will always calculate *Most deprived* minus *Least deprived*, so that a positive difference means higher NO~2~ in the most deprived LSOAs.
:::

## Describing the groups
Before running any test, it is always a good idea to describe and plot the data first. Let us look at the mean and standard deviation of NO~2~ in both groups, and store the difference between the two means as `obs_diff` as we will need it again later:

```{r}
#| label: 07-describe
#| filename: 'R code'
# group summaries
my_sample |>
  group_by(group) |>
  summarise(n = n(),
            mean = mean(no2),
            sd = sd(no2))

# the observed difference in means
obs_diff <- mean(my_sample$no2[my_sample$group == 'Most deprived']) -
  mean(my_sample$no2[my_sample$group == 'Least deprived'])
obs_diff
```

We can then compare the two groups visually with a boxplot:

```{r}
#| label: fig-07-box
#| fig-cap: NO2 in samples of 30 Outer London LSOAs from the most and least income-deprived fifths.
#| filename: 'R code'
boxplot(no2 ~ group, data = my_sample,
        main = 'NO2 in Outer London (samples of 30)',
        xlab = '', ylab = 'Annual mean NO2 (µg/m³)')
```

In our sample, NO~2~ levels are higher in the most deprived LSOAs. However, the two boxes overlap considerably, and last week we saw that sample means vary from one sample to the next. So could a difference this large also appear by chance, even if there were no difference between the two groups in the population?

## Hypotheses
Every hypothesis test starts with a **null hypothesis** (H~0~). This is the 'nothing is going on' explanation, against which we look for evidence. It comes with an **alternative hypothesis** (H~1~). For our question, these are:

- **H~0~**: in the population, mean NO~2~ is the same in both groups, and any difference we see in our sample is due to sampling variability.
- **H~1~**: in the population, mean NO~2~ differs between the two groups.

The test then answers one specific question: *if H~0~ were true, how surprising would the data we observed be?*

## A permutation test
If H~0~ is true, the labels *Most deprived* and *Least deprived* do not tell us anything about NO~2~: any LSOA could just as well have had the other label. This gives us a simple way to see what chance alone can produce. We randomly shuffle the labels, calculate the difference between the two group means again, and repeat this thousands of times. This is called a **permutation test**, and we can run it with `replicate()`, which you used last week:

```{r}
#| label: 07-perm
#| filename: 'R code'
# shuffle the group labels 5,000 times; each time, compute the difference
set.seed(48)
perm_diffs <- replicate(5000, {
  shuffled <- sample(my_sample$group)
  mean(my_sample$no2[shuffled == 'Most deprived']) -
    mean(my_sample$no2[shuffled == 'Least deprived'])
})
```

::: {.callout-note .exercise icon=false}
## Predict first
If the labels are shuffled at random, what do you expect the typical difference between the two groups to be?
:::

Let us plot the 5,000 differences, together with the difference we actually observed:

```{r}
#| label: fig-07-perm
#| fig-cap: Differences in means after shuffling the group labels 5,000 times. The solid red line is the observed difference; the dashed line is the same difference in the other direction.
#| filename: 'R code'
hist(perm_diffs, breaks = 40,
     xlim = range(perm_diffs, obs_diff, -obs_diff),
     main = 'What chance alone produces',
     xlab = 'Difference in mean NO2 (µg/m³)', ylab = 'Number of shuffles',
     col = 'grey80', border = 'white')
abline(v = c(obs_diff, -obs_diff), col = 'red', lty = c(1, 2))
```

Most shuffled differences are close to zero, as we would expect when the labels are meaningless. The **p-value** is the proportion of shuffles that produce a difference at least as large as the one we observed, in either direction:

```{r}
#| label: 07-perm-p
#| filename: 'R code'
# p-value: how often is chance at least as extreme as our data?
mean(abs(perm_diffs) >= abs(obs_diff))
```

Very few shuffles produce a difference as large as ours. In other words, data like ours would be very unlikely if H~0~ were true, so we **reject H~0~** and conclude that the data provide evidence of a difference between the two groups. By convention, a p-value below 0.05 is called *statistically significant*. There is nothing special about 0.05, however, so it is good practice to report the p-value itself.

## Welch's t-test
The t-test does the same job as the permutation test, but uses a formula instead of shuffling. It divides the observed difference by its **standard error**, which we introduced last week:

$$
t = \frac{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}{SE}, \qquad SE = \sqrt{\frac{s_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{s_2^2}{n_2}}
$$

The larger the value of $t$, the further the observed difference is from zero relative to its standard error, and the smaller the p-value. By default, R runs **Welch's t-test**, which does not assume that both groups have the same spread. This makes it a safe choice in most situations. We can run the test with the `t.test()` function:

```{r}
#| label: 07-ttest
#| filename: 'R code'
# Welch two-sample t-test: NO2 by group
t_result <- t.test(no2 ~ group, data = my_sample)
t_result
```

The output contains a lot of information, so let us go through it from the top:

- `t` and `df` are the test statistic and its degrees of freedom. With Welch's test, the degrees of freedom do not need to be a whole number.
- `p-value` should be close to the p-value of our permutation test.
- `95 percent confidence interval` is the confidence interval for the **difference** between the two means.
- `sample estimates` are the means of the two groups.

::: {.callout-tip}
The t-test assumes that the sample means are approximately normally distributed. Thanks to the central limit theorem, which we saw last week, this is usually the case for samples of this size, unless the data are very skewed or contain extreme outliers. The permutation test does not rely on this assumption, which makes it a useful check. Another alternative you may meet in Year 2 is the *Mann-Whitney U test*.
:::

## Effect size: how big is the difference?
A p-value tells us whether a difference can be distinguished from chance, but not whether the difference is **large**. For that, we need the **effect size**. The most useful effect size is often simply the difference itself, in the original units, together with its confidence interval:

```{r}
#| label: 07-effect
#| filename: 'R code'
# difference in means (Most minus Least deprived) and its 95% CI
unname(t_result$estimate[1] - t_result$estimate[2])
t_result$conf.int
```

Is a difference of about 2 µg/m³ large? It helps to compare it with something meaningful: the WHO guideline is 10 µg/m³, and we found a gap of about 4 µg/m³ between Inner and Outer London.

When a variable does not have a natural unit, researchers often use a **standardised** effect size instead, such as **Cohen's d**. This is the difference between the means divided by the (pooled) standard deviation of the two groups:

```{r}
#| label: 07-cohen
#| filename: 'R code'
# Cohen's d: difference in standard deviation units
sds <- my_sample |>
  group_by(group) |>
  summarise(sd = sd(no2))
pooled_sd <- sqrt(mean(sds$sd^2))
obs_diff / pooled_sd
```

As a rough guide, a d of 0.2 is considered *small*, 0.5 *medium* and 0.8 *large*. These labels originally come from psychology, so where possible it is better to judge the size of a difference in its own context.

## Checking against the population
Because we have data for every LSOA, we can do something that is never possible in real research: compare our sample result with the true difference in the population.

```{r}
#| label: 07-truth
#| filename: 'R code'
# the true difference in Outer London
true_diff <- mean(outer$no2[outer$group == 'Most deprived']) -
  mean(outer$no2[outer$group == 'Least deprived'])
true_diff
```

Does the confidence interval from our sample contain the true difference? In real research, we can never check this, which is exactly why reporting the confidence interval matters.

::: {.callout-note .exercise icon=false}
## Try it yourself
Go back to the start of the session, change `set.seed(48)` before `slice_sample()` to a number of your own, and run the sample, the t-test and this check again. Does your new interval contain the true difference? Compare with your neighbours: what share of your intervals would you expect to miss?
:::

## Common misconceptions
Hypothesis tests are easy to run, but also easy to misinterpret. Let us go through four common misconceptions.

### "The p-value is the probability that H~0~ is true"
This is not the case. The p-value is calculated by **assuming** that H~0~ is true: it is the probability of observing data at least as extreme as ours *if* there were no difference. A p-value of 0.01 therefore does not mean that there is a 1% chance that there is no difference.

### "Not significant means no difference"
Let us run the same comparison for Inner London:

```{r}
#| label: 07-inner
#| filename: 'R code'
# the same comparison, in Inner London
inner <- lsoa |>
  filter(inner_outer == 'Inner', income_quintile %in% c(1, 5)) |>
  mutate(group = if_else(income_quintile == 5, 'Most deprived', 'Least deprived'),
         group = factor(group, levels = c('Most deprived', 'Least deprived')))

set.seed(48)
inner_sample <- inner |>
  group_by(group) |>
  slice_sample(n = 30) |>
  ungroup()

t.test(no2 ~ group, data = inner_sample)
```

And compare the result with the true difference in Inner London:

```{r}
#| label: 07-inner-truth
#| filename: 'R code'
# the true difference in Inner London
mean(inner$no2[inner$group == 'Most deprived']) -
  mean(inner$no2[inner$group == 'Least deprived'])
```

The test is not significant, yet there **is** a difference in the population, and it goes in the opposite direction from Outer London (as we saw when we described the data). With 30 LSOAs per group, the test simply could not detect a difference this small. Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence. The confidence interval is helpful here, as it shows the range of differences that are still consistent with our data, including the true one.

### "Significant means important"
With enough data, even a very small difference becomes statistically significant. Let us compare the 4th and 5th income deprivation quintiles across London, this time with large samples of 800 LSOAs each:

```{r}
#| label: 07-large-n
#| filename: 'R code'
# a small difference, large samples
large <- lsoa |>
  filter(income_quintile %in% c(4, 5)) |>
  mutate(group = factor(income_quintile))

set.seed(48)
large_sample <- large |>
  group_by(group) |>
  slice_sample(n = 800) |>
  ungroup()

t.test(no2 ~ group, data = large_sample)
```

The p-value is small, but the difference is only about half a µg/m³. The result is statistically significant, but hardly important, which is why we should always report the effect size and not only the p-value.

### "Test enough things and report the significant one"
Even when H~0~ is true, a test at the 0.05 level will still come out significant 5% of the time. We can see this by drawing two samples from the **same** group 1,000 times, so that H~0~ is true every time, and counting how many of the tests are significant.

::: {.callout-note .exercise icon=false}
## Predict first
Before you run the code, write down how many of the 1,000 tests you expect to be significant.
:::

```{r}
#| label: 07-multiple
#| filename: 'R code'
# 1,000 tests where there is no difference at all
same_group <- lsoa |>
  filter(inner_outer == 'Outer', income_quintile == 3)

set.seed(48)
p_values <- replicate(1000, {
  a <- sample(same_group$no2, 30)
  b <- sample(same_group$no2, 30)
  t.test(a, b)$p.value
})

# how many are 'significant', and what share?
sum(p_values < 0.05)
mean(p_values < 0.05)
```

About one in twenty tests produces a 'finding' from pure noise. If you were to compare all 33 boroughs with each other (528 pairs), you would find many significant differences, whether or not they mean anything. It is therefore important to decide what you will test **before** you look at the data, and to report every test you ran.

::: {.callout-warning}
There are two more things a test cannot do. First, it cannot tell us **why** groups differ: location in Inner or Outer London, road networks and housing all play a role. Second, our data describe **areas**, not people: the average NO~2~ in an LSOA is not the exposure of every resident who lives there. Drawing conclusions about individuals from data about areas is known as the *ecological fallacy*.
:::

## Reporting your results
When you report a comparison between two groups, for instance in an essay or a worksheet, include the descriptive statistics for both groups, the result of the test, the size of the difference with its confidence interval, and what this means in plain words. Report exact p-values (or *p* < 0.001 for very small values) rather than only stating that a result is significant. Based on this session's samples, this could look as follows:

> In random samples of 30 Outer London LSOAs per group, mean annual NO~2~ was `r sprintf('%.1f', t_result$estimate[1])` µg/m³ in the most income-deprived fifth and `r sprintf('%.1f', t_result$estimate[2])` µg/m³ in the least deprived fifth. The difference of `r sprintf('%.1f', obs_diff)` µg/m³ (95% CI `r sprintf('%.1f', t_result$conf.int[1])` to `r sprintf('%.1f', t_result$conf.int[2])`) is unlikely to be due to sampling variability alone (Welch's t = `r sprintf('%.2f', t_result$statistic)`, df = `r sprintf('%.1f', t_result$parameter)`, p = `r sprintf('%.3f', t_result$p.value)`; permutation test p = `r sprintf('%.3f', mean(abs(perm_diffs) >= abs(obs_diff)))`). This is a difference of about `r sprintf('%.1f', obs_diff / pooled_sd)` standard deviations, but small next to the gap between Inner and Outer London. In Outer London, more deprived areas are exposed to somewhat higher NO~2~; the data do not tell us why.

::: {.callout-note .exercise icon=false}
## Try it yourself
Choose **one** other comparison, for example PM~2.5~ instead of NO~2~, or two boroughs. Write down H~0~ and H~1~ **before** you look at the data, and then work through the same steps: describe, test, effect size and report.
:::

## Looking ahead
Over these three sessions, you have learned to describe data, to estimate with uncertainty, and to test for a difference between two groups. In Year 2 methods modules, you will build on this foundation with more advanced statistical techniques.

## Before you leave
By the end of this session, you should have:

- [ ] saved your script as `w07-testing.R`;
- [ ] stated H~0~ and H~1~ for a comparison of two groups;
- [ ] run a permutation test, with its histogram and p-value, and a Welch's t-test on the same comparison;
- [ ] reported the difference in means with its 95% confidence interval, and Cohen's d;
- [ ] explained each of the four misconceptions in your own words;
- [ ] reported a comparison of your own choice.

## Troubleshooting
| Problem | What to try |
| :------ | :---------- |
| `grouping factor must have exactly 2 levels` | Your data contain more (or fewer) than two groups. Check your `filter()`, and run `count(my_sample, group)`. |
| The difference has the wrong sign | Check the order in `factor(..., levels = ...)`: R reports the first level minus the second. |
| `object 'outer' not found` | Run your script from the top. |
| My p-values differ slightly from the page | The permutation p-value depends on the random shuffles. Re-run `set.seed(48)` directly before `replicate()`. |
